name: Provençal Lentils Roasted
description: Tender lentils roasted in garlic-marinated style, packed with 0g carbs and 54g protein per serving.
tips: Use the marinade without extra oil to keep calories in check. Each serving delivers 54g protein to support muscle preservation while in a deficit.
ingredients_items: lentils|eggplant|artichoke hearts|cucumber|roasted garlic|couscous|feta cheese|coriander|rosemary|mint|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Preheat the oven to 120 °C / 250 °F. Low-temperature roasting cooks the protein edge to edge at a uniform temperature — a technique popularised by Heston Blumenthal and J. Kenji López-Alt.
step_2: Season the protein generously and place on a wire rack set over a rimmed baking tray. The rack elevates it, allowing hot air to circulate underneath for even cooking.
step_3: Slow-roast until the internal temperature reaches 10 °C below your target: 47 °C / 117 °F for medium-rare beef; 64 °C / 147 °F for chicken; 58 °C / 136 °F for fish. This takes 45–90 minutes for smaller cuts, 2–4 hours for large roasts.
step_4: Remove from the oven and tent loosely with foil. Meanwhile, heat a skillet or increase oven to 260 °C / 500 °F broil setting. This is the reverse sear — the exterior browns in 60–90 seconds without affecting the already-perfect interior.
step_5: Sear the protein in the scorching-hot pan for 60–90 seconds per side, or under the broiler 5 cm from the element for 2–3 minutes per side, until the crust is deep brown.
step_6: Rest for only 5 minutes — since the interior was cooked slowly, less resting is needed. The juices are already set.
step_7: Carve and serve immediately with pan drippings, the prepared sauce, and roasted vegetables.

tips: Pair with an additional portion of orzo pasta to add 150–200 extra quality calories for a bulk phase.
ingredients_items: shrimp|fresh parsley|eggplant|arugula|walnuts|rosemary|sumac|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Preheat the oven to 220 °C / 430 °F fan-forced (or 240 °C / 465 °F conventional). High heat is what distinguishes roasting from baking — it drives moisture from the surface before it can inhibit caramelisation.
step_2: Prepare the marinade: mix oil, acid (lemon/vinegar), spices, and aromatics. Coat the protein and vegetables thoroughly. Spread in a single layer on a large sheet pan — never overlap. Crowding creates steam and prevents browning.
step_3: Roast on the upper-middle rack for 20 minutes undisturbed. Resist the urge to open the oven — each opening drops the temperature 10–15 °C and adds minutes.
step_4: After 20 minutes, flip the protein and toss the vegetables. Return for a further 10–15 minutes until the protein is cooked through and the vegetables are caramelised at the edges.
step_5: Scatter any delicate additions (fresh tomatoes, herbs, olives) in the last 5 minutes — they need only to warm and soften, not cook.
step_6: Test doneness: the protein should register target temperature on a thermometer, and the juices should run clear when pierced at the thickest point. The vegetables should be tender with darkened edges.
step_7: Serve directly from the pan or transfer to a platter. Drizzle with good olive oil, squeeze over fresh citrus, and scatter with fresh herbs and any garnishes immediately before serving.

name: Lebanese Lemon-Infused Halloumi Cheese Soup
description: A medium mediterranean soup featuring halloumi cheese cooked poached with thyme, mint and fresh spinach.
tips: Pair with an additional portion of orzo pasta to add 150–200 extra quality calories for a bulk phase.
ingredients_items: halloumi cheese|spinach|arugula|roasted garlic|feta cheese|thyme|mint|za'atar|rosemary|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Prepare the poaching liquid (court-bouillon): combine water, wine or vinegar, aromatics (bay leaf, peppercorns, thyme, onion), and salt. Bring to a boil and simmer 15 minutes to develop flavour. Taste — it should be pleasantly seasoned.
step_2: Reduce the poaching liquid to a gentle simmer: 70–80 °C / 158–176 °F. At this temperature the liquid barely moves, with small bubbles rising from the base only. Full boiling agitates and breaks delicate proteins.
step_3: Lower the protein into the warm liquid gently. It should be fully submerged. Adjust heat to maintain 75 °C / 167 °F — use a thermometer. The liquid should never reach a boil.
step_4: Poach for 8–15 minutes depending on thickness. Fish (2.5 cm) takes 8–10 minutes; chicken breast (200 g) takes 12–15 minutes. Test with a thermometer: fish at 60 °C / 140 °F; chicken at 74 °C / 165 °F.
step_5: Remove with a slotted spoon or spider and drain. Pat gently dry if a sauce is to be applied — excess water dilutes sauces.
step_6: Reduce the poaching liquid by half over medium-high heat to concentrate its flavour. Whisk in cold butter piece by piece off the heat to create a beurre blanc, or reduce fully for a glaze.
step_7: Plate the protein and spoon the concentrated sauce around the base. Garnish with fresh herbs and serve immediately.

name: Sun-Kissed Main Course with Eggs and Dill
description: A turkish classic reimagined with eggs and aromatic dill — perfect for dinner.
tips: Weigh your eggs raw — cooked weight loss varies. Hitting 44g protein per serving keeps you full despite the calorie restriction.
ingredients_items: eggs|roasted red pepper|artichoke hearts|capers|whole wheat pita|extra virgin olive oil|dill|mint|rosemary|oregano|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Remove the protein from the refrigerator 20–30 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Cold protein dropped into a hot pan drops the pan temperature dramatically, resulting in steaming rather than searing.
step_2: Heat a heavy stainless-steel or cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat for 2–3 minutes until a water droplet dances and evaporates immediately. Add a thin film of neutral oil (grapeseed or sunflower) and heat until shimmering, just before smoking — approximately 200 °C / 400 °F.
step_3: Season the protein generously with flaky salt and fresh pepper on all sides immediately before it goes into the pan — not earlier, as salt draws moisture to the surface.
step_4: Lay the protein in the pan away from you to avoid oil splatter. Press gently with a spatula for 5 seconds to ensure full contact. Sear undisturbed for 3–4 minutes on medium-high heat until a deep golden-brown crust releases naturally from the pan.
step_5: Flip once. Add 2 tablespoons of butter, 2 garlic cloves, and a thyme sprig to the pan. Tilt the pan at a 30° angle and baste the protein continuously with the foaming butter for 90 seconds — this bastes, flavours, and accelerates cooking simultaneously.
step_6: Check doneness: fish flakes at 60–63 °C / 140–145 °F; chicken breast at 74 °C / 165 °F; duck breast at 57 °C / 135 °F (medium-rare). Use a thermometer — visual cues alone are unreliable.
step_7: Transfer to a wire rack set over a plate. Rest 3–5 minutes. Deglaze the pan with a splash of wine or stock, scraping up all fond (browned bits) to build an instant pan sauce. Pour over and serve.

step_2: Season the protein generously and place on a wire rack set over a rimmed baking tray. The rack elevates it, allowing hot air to circulate underneath for even cooking.

step_4: Remove from the oven and tent loosely with foil. Meanwhile, heat a skillet or increase oven to 260 °C / 500 °F broil setting. This is the reverse sear — the exterior browns in 60–90 seconds without affecting the already-perfect interior.
step_5: Sear the protein in the scorching-hot pan for 60–90 seconds per side, or under the broiler 5 cm from the element for 2–3 minutes per side, until the crust is deep brown.
step_6: Rest for only 5 minutes — since the interior was cooked slowly, less resting is needed. The juices are already set.
step_7: Carve and serve immediately with pan drippings, the prepared sauce, and roasted vegetables.

name: Slow-Roasted Grilled Chicken Breast with Cherry Tomatoes
description: A hard mediterranean snack featuring grilled chicken breast cooked grilled with za'atar, coriander and fresh cherry tomatoes.

step_4: Flip once and sear the second side for 2 minutes. Move to the indirect side, close the lid, and cook to the target internal temperature: 63 °C / 145 °F for fish; 74 °C / 165 °F for poultry; 57 °C / 135 °F for medium-rare beef or lamb.
step_5: While the protein finishes, grill the vegetables over direct medium heat (180 °C / 350 °F) for 3–5 minutes per side until lightly charred and just tender.
step_6: Rest the protein on a warm plate, tented loosely with foil, for 5 minutes (steaks) or 3 minutes (fish, chicken breast). Resting allows juices to redistribute — cutting too early loses up to 30 % of moisture.
step_7: Slice against the grain if applicable, arrange over the vegetables, and finish with the prepared sauce and fresh herbs immediately before serving.

step_1: Prepare the aromatics: bruise lemongrass stalks with the back of a knife to release the oils. Tear kaffir lime leaves. These will infuse the steam with their volatile aromatics.

step_7: Transfer to a serving plate with all the aromatic juices. Finish with fresh herb leaves, a squeeze of lime, and a drizzle of sauce at the table.

name: Teriyaki-Style Yellowtail with Snow Peas
description: A hokkaido classic reimagined with yellowtail and aromatic ponzu — perfect for breakfast.
tips: Balanced macros make this a reliable daily staple. Rotate between this and other protein sources across the week for variety.
ingredients_items: yellowtail|snow peas|daikon radish|sesame oil|ponzu|dashi|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Pound or process the aromatics (garlic, chili, lemongrass, galangal) into a rough paste. In Thai cooking, this paste is the flavour engine of the dish — do not shortcut with pre-made pastes.
step_2: Prepare the sauce: combine fish sauce, palm sugar, lime juice, and any stock in a small bowl. Balance the four elements — salt, sweet, sour, and a suggestion of bitterness. Taste and adjust before cooking.
step_3: Heat the wok over maximum heat for 2 minutes. Add oil and heat until smoking. Fry the paste over high heat for 60–90 seconds, pressing and stirring, until it turns from pale to golden and the raw aroma softens into something fragrant and complex.
step_4: Add the protein to the paste. Stir-fry over high heat for 2–3 minutes, ensuring the paste coats every surface. Add a tablespoon of water if the paste sticks.
step_5: Add the vegetables in order of firmness. Stir-fry 2 minutes until just tender-crisp. Add the sauce mixture and toss for 30 seconds over high heat until every component is glazed.
step_6: Add fresh herbs (Thai basil, holy basil) off the heat — the residual heat is sufficient to wilt them without destroying their volatile aromatics.
step_7: Serve immediately over jasmine rice. Provide lime wedges, fish sauce, palm sugar, and dried chili at the table for individual adjustment.

tips: Pair with an additional portion of sourdough bread to add 150–200 extra quality calories for a bulk phase.
ingredients_items: cod fillet|butternut squash|sweet potato|brussels sprouts|pasta|cheddar cheese|garlic powder|cayenne|liquid smoke|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Preheat a charcoal or gas grill to high heat, 260 °C / 500 °F. A properly heated grill grate should cause a drop of water to evaporate in under 1 second.
step_2: Prepare a basting mixture of your sauce ingredients. Pat the protein dry, season lightly — over-seasoning can burn on a high-heat grill before the interior cooks.
step_3: Oil the grate and lay the protein down. Grill uncovered for 90 seconds, then rotate 45° to create a crosshatch; grill 90 seconds more. Flip and repeat on the second side.
step_4: Brush the first layer of baste on the cooked surface and close the lid for 1 minute to set the glaze. Open, baste again, and grill uncovered 30 seconds until caramelised and lightly charred at the edges.
step_5: Check internal temperature — target 60 °C / 140 °F for salmon (medium), 63 °C / 145 °F for white fish, 74 °C / 165 °F for chicken. The flesh should spring back when pressed.
step_6: Transfer to a warm board and rest 3 minutes. This is non-negotiable even for fish — the carryover continues cooking 2–3 °C after removal from heat.
step_7: Plate over prepared vegetables or grains, spoon the remaining baste around the base, and scatter fresh herbs and condiment.

name: Cajun-style Maple-Smoked Chicken Wings Salad
description: A cajun-style classic reimagined with chicken wings and aromatic hot sauce — perfect for lunch.
tips: Pair with an additional portion of sourdough bread to add 150–200 extra quality calories for a bulk phase.
ingredients_items: chicken wings|iceberg lettuce|sweet corn|coleslaw mix|peanut butter|hot sauce|apple cider vinegar|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Set up a two-zone grill: ignite one side to high heat (230–260 °C / 450–500 °F) and leave the other side unlit for indirect cooking. Let the grill heat for 10 minutes with the lid closed.
step_2: While the grill heats, pat the protein completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season generously with salt, pepper, and spices on all sides; press the seasoning in firmly.
step_3: Brush the grill grates with a high-smoke-point oil (grapeseed or refined avocado). Place the protein on the hot side. Do not move it for 2–3 minutes until grill marks release naturally — forcing it tears the crust.
step_4: Flip once and sear the second side for 2 minutes. Move to the indirect side, close the lid, and cook to the target internal temperature: 63 °C / 145 °F for fish; 74 °C / 165 °F for poultry; 57 °C / 135 °F for medium-rare beef or lamb.
step_5: While the protein finishes, grill the vegetables over direct medium heat (180 °C / 350 °F) for 3–5 minutes per side until lightly charred and just tender.
step_6: Rest the protein on a warm plate, tented loosely with foil, for 5 minutes (steaks) or 3 minutes (fish, chicken breast). Resting allows juices to redistribute — cutting too early loses up to 30 % of moisture.
step_7: Slice against the grain if applicable, arrange over the vegetables, and finish with the prepared sauce and fresh herbs immediately before serving.

step_1: Preheat the oven to 160 °C / 325 °F — low enough to dissolve collagen into gelatin over time without toughening the muscle fibres. Pat the protein completely dry; wet protein will steam, not brown.
step_2: Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat, 200 °C / 400 °F on the surface. Brown the protein in batches for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply mahogany. This Maillard reaction creates the complex flavour base for the entire braise.
step_3: Remove the protein. Reduce heat to medium and sauté the mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery or regional equivalent) for 5–7 minutes, stirring, until softened and lightly coloured. Season lightly.
step_4: Add tomato paste or spice paste and stir for 1–2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick — cooking out the raw taste. Deglaze with wine, stock, or water and scrape all the fond from the bottom.
step_5: Nestle the protein into the braising liquid. The liquid should reach halfway up the protein, never submerge it — you are braising, not boiling. Bring to a gentle simmer on the stovetop.
step_6: Cover with a tight lid and transfer to the oven. Braise for 1.5–3 hours depending on the cut — it is done when a fork slides in and twists with zero resistance, not just when it's tender. Turn the protein every 45 minutes for even cooking.
step_7: Remove the protein. Strain the braising liquid, skim the fat, and reduce over medium-high heat for 5–8 minutes until glossy and sauce-like. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve the protein with sauce spooned over and fresh herbs.

tips: Pair with an additional portion of lentilles du Puy to add 150–200 extra quality calories for a bulk phase.
ingredients_items: salmon fillet|fennel fenouil|tomatoes tomates|turnip navets|leeks poireaux|farro wheat|crème fraîche|herbes de Provence|tarragon estragon|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Preheat oven to 200 °C / 400 °F. Cut a large piece of baking parchment — roughly 3× the size of the protein portion. Fold it in half to mark the centre.
step_2: On one half of the parchment, build a base of aromatics and vegetables. Set the seasoned protein on top. Spoon the sauce or flavoured butter over the surface and add any finishing aromatics.
step_3: Fold the parchment over the protein. Starting from one corner, make overlapping half-moon folds around the edge to create a sealed parcel. Twist the final fold tightly to lock in the steam.
step_4: Place the parcels on a baking tray. Bake for 12–18 minutes depending on protein thickness. The parcel will puff dramatically — this is the steam building inside, cooking the protein in its own aromatic juices at approximately 100 °C / 212 °F internal environment.
step_5: The parcel is done when it is fully puffed and beginning to turn golden. Do not open to check — trust the timing and use an instant-read probe through the parchment if uncertain.
step_6: Bring the sealed parcels directly to the table — the ceremony of opening at the table, releasing a cloud of aromatic steam, is half the pleasure. Cut open with scissors.
step_7: Serve immediately with crusty bread to absorb the juices that pool in the base of the parcel.

step_1: Prepare the poaching liquid (court-bouillon): combine water, wine or vinegar, aromatics (bay leaf, peppercorns, thyme, onion), and salt. Bring to a boil and simmer 15 minutes to develop flavour. Taste — it should be pleasantly seasoned.
step_2: Reduce the poaching liquid to a gentle simmer: 70–80 °C / 158–176 °F. At this temperature the liquid barely moves, with small bubbles rising from the base only. Full boiling agitates and breaks delicate proteins.
step_3: Lower the protein into the warm liquid gently. It should be fully submerged. Adjust heat to maintain 75 °C / 167 °F — use a thermometer. The liquid should never reach a boil.
step_4: Poach for 8–15 minutes depending on thickness. Fish (2.5 cm) takes 8–10 minutes; chicken breast (200 g) takes 12–15 minutes. Test with a thermometer: fish at 60 °C / 140 °F; chicken at 74 °C / 165 °F.
step_5: Remove with a slotted spoon or spider and drain. Pat gently dry if a sauce is to be applied — excess water dilutes sauces.
step_6: Reduce the poaching liquid by half over medium-high heat to concentrate its flavour. Whisk in cold butter piece by piece off the heat to create a beurre blanc, or reduce fully for a glaze.
step_7: Plate the protein and spoon the concentrated sauce around the base. Garnish with fresh herbs and serve immediately.

name: Alsatian Chicken Supreme Grilled

step_2: While the grill heats, pat the protein completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season generously with salt, pepper, and spices on all sides; press the seasoning in firmly.
step_3: Brush the grill grates with a high-smoke-point oil (grapeseed or refined avocado). Place the protein on the hot side. Do not move it for 2–3 minutes until grill marks release naturally — forcing it tears the crust.
step_4: Flip once and sear the second side for 2 minutes. Move to the indirect side, close the lid, and cook to the target internal temperature: 63 °C / 145 °F for fish; 74 °C / 165 °F for poultry; 57 °C / 135 °F for medium-rare beef or lamb.
step_5: While the protein finishes, grill the vegetables over direct medium heat (180 °C / 350 °F) for 3–5 minutes per side until lightly charred and just tender.

step_3: Reduce to medium heat. Cook the aromatics (onion, garlic, ginger) in the same oil for 8–10 minutes, stirring often, until deeply softened and golden — not just translucent. Under-cooked aromatics leave a raw, harsh flavour.
step_4: Add the ground spices and tomato or tamarind base. Stir constantly for 2 minutes over medium heat, frying the paste until it darkens and pulls away from the sides of the pot.
step_5: Return the protein. Add enough warm liquid (stock, coconut milk, or tomato) to reach halfway up the sides. Bring to a bubbling simmer, then reduce heat to the lowest possible setting — the surface should barely tremor.

step_1: Preheat a charcoal or gas grill to high heat, 260 °C / 500 °F. A properly heated grill grate should cause a drop of water to evaporate in under 1 second.
step_2: Prepare a basting mixture of your sauce ingredients. Pat the protein dry, season lightly — over-seasoning can burn on a high-heat grill before the interior cooks.
step_3: Oil the grate and lay the protein down. Grill uncovered for 90 seconds, then rotate 45° to create a crosshatch; grill 90 seconds more. Flip and repeat on the second side.
step_4: Brush the first layer of baste on the cooked surface and close the lid for 1 minute to set the glaze. Open, baste again, and grill uncovered 30 seconds until caramelised and lightly charred at the edges.
step_5: Check internal temperature — target 60 °C / 140 °F for salmon (medium), 63 °C / 145 °F for white fish, 74 °C / 165 °F for chicken. The flesh should spring back when pressed.
step_6: Transfer to a warm board and rest 3 minutes. This is non-negotiable even for fish — the carryover continues cooking 2–3 °C after removal from heat.
step_7: Plate over prepared vegetables or grains, spoon the remaining baste around the base, and scatter fresh herbs and condiment.

name: Beurre-Blanc-Finished Mussels Moules with Watercress Cresson
description: A medium french breakfast featuring mussels moules cooked braised with white wine, Dijon mustard and fresh watercress cresson.

ingredients_items: mussels moules|watercress cresson|spinach épinards|potato gratin|crème fraîche|white wine|Dijon mustard|herbes de Provence|flat parsley|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Preheat the oven to 160 °C / 325 °F — low enough to dissolve collagen into gelatin over time without toughening the muscle fibres. Pat the protein completely dry; wet protein will steam, not brown.
step_2: Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat, 200 °C / 400 °F on the surface. Brown the protein in batches for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply mahogany. This Maillard reaction creates the complex flavour base for the entire braise.
step_3: Remove the protein. Reduce heat to medium and sauté the mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery or regional equivalent) for 5–7 minutes, stirring, until softened and lightly coloured. Season lightly.
step_4: Add tomato paste or spice paste and stir for 1–2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick — cooking out the raw taste. Deglaze with wine, stock, or water and scrape all the fond from the bottom.
step_5: Nestle the protein into the braising liquid. The liquid should reach halfway up the protein, never submerge it — you are braising, not boiling. Bring to a gentle simmer on the stovetop.
step_6: Cover with a tight lid and transfer to the oven. Braise for 1.5–3 hours depending on the cut — it is done when a fork slides in and twists with zero resistance, not just when it's tender. Turn the protein every 45 minutes for even cooking.
step_7: Remove the protein. Strain the braising liquid, skim the fat, and reduce over medium-high heat for 5–8 minutes until glossy and sauce-like. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve the protein with sauce spooned over and fresh herbs.

step_1: Prepare the poaching liquid (court-bouillon): combine water, wine or vinegar, aromatics (bay leaf, peppercorns, thyme, onion), and salt. Bring to a boil and simmer 15 minutes to develop flavour. Taste — it should be pleasantly seasoned.
step_2: Reduce the poaching liquid to a gentle simmer: 70–80 °C / 158–176 °F. At this temperature the liquid barely moves, with small bubbles rising from the base only. Full boiling agitates and breaks delicate proteins.
step_3: Lower the protein into the warm liquid gently. It should be fully submerged. Adjust heat to maintain 75 °C / 167 °F — use a thermometer. The liquid should never reach a boil.
step_4: Poach for 8–15 minutes depending on thickness. Fish (2.5 cm) takes 8–10 minutes; chicken breast (200 g) takes 12–15 minutes. Test with a thermometer: fish at 60 °C / 140 °F; chicken at 74 °C / 165 °F.
step_5: Remove with a slotted spoon or spider and drain. Pat gently dry if a sauce is to be applied — excess water dilutes sauces.
step_6: Reduce the poaching liquid by half over medium-high heat to concentrate its flavour. Whisk in cold butter piece by piece off the heat to create a beurre blanc, or reduce fully for a glaze.
step_7: Plate the protein and spoon the concentrated sauce around the base. Garnish with fresh herbs and serve immediately.

step_1: Preheat the oven to 120 °C / 250 °F. Low-temperature roasting cooks the protein edge to edge at a uniform temperature — a technique popularised by Heston Blumenthal and J. Kenji López-Alt.

step_3: Slow-roast until the internal temperature reaches 10 °C below your target: 47 °C / 117 °F for medium-rare beef; 64 °C / 147 °F for chicken; 58 °C / 136 °F for fish. This takes 45–90 minutes for smaller cuts, 2–4 hours for large roasts.
step_4: Remove from the oven and tent loosely with foil. Meanwhile, heat a skillet or increase oven to 260 °C / 500 °F broil setting. This is the reverse sear — the exterior browns in 60–90 seconds without affecting the already-perfect interior.
step_5: Sear the protein in the scorching-hot pan for 60–90 seconds per side, or under the broiler 5 cm from the element for 2–3 minutes per side, until the crust is deep brown.
step_6: Rest for only 5 minutes — since the interior was cooked slowly, less resting is needed. The juices are already set.
step_7: Carve and serve immediately with pan drippings, the prepared sauce, and roasted vegetables.

tips: Use the marinade without extra oil to keep calories in check. Each serving delivers 32g protein to support muscle preservation while in a deficit.
ingredients_items: cuttlefish sepia|roasted tomato|piquillo peppers|spinach espinacas|Manchego cheese|saffron|Rioja wine|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Heat the oven to 150 °C / 300 °F. In Italian slow-cooking, lower and slower is always better — the goal is collagen-to-gelatin conversion, which requires 2+ hours at 80–95 °C / 176–203 °F.
step_2: In a heavy oven-safe casserole, heat olive oil over medium heat and sauté the soffritto (onion, celery, carrot) for 10 full minutes, stirring frequently, until golden and sweet — this is the foundation of Italian braising. Do not rush it.
step_3: Raise heat to medium-high. Add the seasoned protein and sear 3–4 minutes per side. Remove. Add the tomatoes or wine, scrape the fond, and bring to a boil for 2 minutes.
step_4: Return the protein. The liquid should not cover the protein — add just enough to come halfway up. Tuck in fresh herbs and a Parmesan rind if available (it enriches the sauce with glutamates).
step_5: Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 2–3 hours. Every hour, turn the protein and baste with the surrounding juices. A properly braised Italian stew barely moves in the pot — it should tremble, not bubble.
step_6: When done, the protein yields instantly to a fork and the sauce is glossy and reduced. Adjust seasoning with salt and, if too acidic, a small pinch of sugar.
step_7: Serve over polenta, hand-cut pappardelle, or with crusty bread to capture every drop of the sauce. Always finish with the best olive oil you own and fresh herbs.

step_1: Prepare a herb crust: combine fresh herbs, garlic, zest, and a tablespoon of olive oil into a rough paste. Press firmly onto the top surface of the protein.
step_2: Preheat the grill to medium heat, 175–190 °C / 350–375 °F. Lower heat allows the herb crust to toast without burning and lets thicker cuts cook through.
step_3: Place the protein crust-side up on the grill (indirect if using gas) and cook with the lid closed for 8–12 minutes, depending on thickness — approximately 10 minutes per 2.5 cm / 1 inch.
step_4: Carefully flip and grill the crust side for 2–3 minutes over direct heat until golden and fragrant. Watch closely — herbs burn in seconds over high heat.
step_5: Verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest point away from bone. Target temperatures: 74 °C / 165 °F chicken; 70 °C / 158 °F pork; 63 °C / 145 °F fish.
step_6: Rest 5 minutes before slicing. The crust will firm and adhere better after resting, making clean slices possible.
step_7: Serve over the dressed vegetables or salad, with a wedge of citrus and a drizzle of best-quality finishing oil.

name: Al Ajillo Garlic-Style Snack with Rabbit Conejo and Sherry Vinegar
description: A aragonese classic reimagined with rabbit conejo and aromatic sherry vinegar — perfect for snack.

ingredients_items: rabbit conejo|piquillo peppers|roasted tomato|extra virgin olive oil|sherry vinegar|garlic|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Set up a two-zone grill: ignite one side to high heat (230–260 °C / 450–500 °F) and leave the other side unlit for indirect cooking. Let the grill heat for 10 minutes with the lid closed.
step_2: While the grill heats, pat the protein completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season generously with salt, pepper, and spices on all sides; press the seasoning in firmly.
step_3: Brush the grill grates with a high-smoke-point oil (grapeseed or refined avocado). Place the protein on the hot side. Do not move it for 2–3 minutes until grill marks release naturally — forcing it tears the crust.
step_4: Flip once and sear the second side for 2 minutes. Move to the indirect side, close the lid, and cook to the target internal temperature: 63 °C / 145 °F for fish; 74 °C / 165 °F for poultry; 57 °C / 135 °F for medium-rare beef or lamb.
step_5: While the protein finishes, grill the vegetables over direct medium heat (180 °C / 350 °F) for 3–5 minutes per side until lightly charred and just tender.
step_6: Rest the protein on a warm plate, tented loosely with foil, for 5 minutes (steaks) or 3 minutes (fish, chicken breast). Resting allows juices to redistribute — cutting too early loses up to 30 % of moisture.
step_7: Slice against the grain if applicable, arrange over the vegetables, and finish with the prepared sauce and fresh herbs immediately before serving.

tips: Balanced macros make this a reliable daily staple. Rotate between this and other protein sources across the week for variety.
ingredients_items: tempeh-style fermented tofu|snow peas|bok choy|shiitake mushrooms|Chinese broccoli gai lan|wood ear fungus|fried rice base|Sichuan chili oil|dark soy sauce|Shaoxing wine|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Blanch the protein in boiling water for 3 minutes to remove impurities and excess blood. Drain, rinse under cold water, and pat dry — this step is standard across Chinese, Japanese, and Korean braised-meat traditions.
step_2: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a wok or heavy pot over high heat. Add aromatics and stir-fry 30 seconds. Add Shaoxing wine or mirin, let it sizzle and reduce by half — about 30 seconds.
step_3: Add the braising liquid components: soy or tamari, sweet soy or palm sugar, star anise, cinnamon, ginger, and enough water or stock to half-submerge the protein. Bring to a strong boil.
step_4: Add the protein, reduce heat to medium-low, and braise partially covered for 1–2 hours, turning every 30 minutes. The liquid should simmer steadily — bubbling around the edges but not vigorously boiling, approximately 90–95 °C / 194–203 °F.
step_5: Remove the lid for the final 20 minutes and raise heat to medium. The sauce will reduce and coat the protein in a lacquered, glossy glaze — this finishing step is critical for the signature texture.
step_6: Check doneness: the protein should be pull-apart tender and the sauce should coat a spoon thickly. Remove aromatics (star anise, cinnamon) before serving.
step_7: Serve over steamed jasmine rice or hand-cut noodles. Spoon sauce generously over the top and finish with sliced spring onions and a drizzle of sesame oil.

name: Cantonese Wok-Tossed Pork Belly Wuhua Rou Soup
description: Tender pork belly wuhua rou slow cooked in wok-tossed style, packed with 0g carbs and 36g protein per serving.

ingredients_items: pork belly wuhua rou|bok choy|wood ear fungus|bean sprouts|shiitake mushrooms|rice congee base|toasted sesame oil|oyster sauce|star anise|dark soy sauce|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Heat the oven to 150 °C / 300 °F. In Italian slow-cooking, lower and slower is always better — the goal is collagen-to-gelatin conversion, which requires 2+ hours at 80–95 °C / 176–203 °F.
step_2: In a heavy oven-safe casserole, heat olive oil over medium heat and sauté the soffritto (onion, celery, carrot) for 10 full minutes, stirring frequently, until golden and sweet — this is the foundation of Italian braising. Do not rush it.
step_3: Raise heat to medium-high. Add the seasoned protein and sear 3–4 minutes per side. Remove. Add the tomatoes or wine, scrape the fond, and bring to a boil for 2 minutes.
step_4: Return the protein. The liquid should not cover the protein — add just enough to come halfway up. Tuck in fresh herbs and a Parmesan rind if available (it enriches the sauce with glutamates).
step_5: Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 2–3 hours. Every hour, turn the protein and baste with the surrounding juices. A properly braised Italian stew barely moves in the pot — it should tremble, not bubble.
step_6: When done, the protein yields instantly to a fork and the sauce is glossy and reduced. Adjust seasoning with salt and, if too acidic, a small pinch of sugar.
step_7: Serve over polenta, hand-cut pappardelle, or with crusty bread to capture every drop of the sauce. Always finish with the best olive oil you own and fresh herbs.

step_3: Remove the protein. Reduce heat to medium and sauté the mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery or regional equivalent) for 5–7 minutes, stirring, until softened and lightly coloured. Season lightly.

step_1: Heat the oven to 150 °C / 300 °F. In Italian slow-cooking, lower and slower is always better — the goal is collagen-to-gelatin conversion, which requires 2+ hours at 80–95 °C / 176–203 °F.
step_2: In a heavy oven-safe casserole, heat olive oil over medium heat and sauté the soffritto (onion, celery, carrot) for 10 full minutes, stirring frequently, until golden and sweet — this is the foundation of Italian braising. Do not rush it.
step_3: Raise heat to medium-high. Add the seasoned protein and sear 3–4 minutes per side. Remove. Add the tomatoes or wine, scrape the fond, and bring to a boil for 2 minutes.
step_4: Return the protein. The liquid should not cover the protein — add just enough to come halfway up. Tuck in fresh herbs and a Parmesan rind if available (it enriches the sauce with glutamates).
step_5: Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 2–3 hours. Every hour, turn the protein and baste with the surrounding juices. A properly braised Italian stew barely moves in the pot — it should tremble, not bubble.
step_6: When done, the protein yields instantly to a fork and the sauce is glossy and reduced. Adjust seasoning with salt and, if too acidic, a small pinch of sugar.
step_7: Serve over polenta, hand-cut pappardelle, or with crusty bread to capture every drop of the sauce. Always finish with the best olive oil you own and fresh herbs.

step_1: Prepare all ingredients before any heat is applied — stir-frying happens in under 5 minutes and there is no time to stop and cut once you begin. Slice protein thinly (5 mm / ¼ inch), cut vegetables to uniform size.
step_2: Season the protein: toss with 1 teaspoon cornstarch, a pinch of salt, and a dash of soy sauce. The cornstarch creates a light coating that protects moisture and helps the sauce cling.
step_3: Heat a seasoned wok over the highest possible flame — a properly heated wok surface reaches 300–370 °C / 570–700 °F. Add 2 tablespoons of oil in a clockwise swirl around the sides. When thin wisps of smoke rise from the oil, the wok is ready.
step_4: Add the aromatics (garlic, ginger, dried chili). Stir constantly for 15–20 seconds — aromatics burn in 30 seconds at this temperature. Their fragrance signals they are ready.
step_5: Add the protein in a single layer. Do not stir for 60 seconds — let it sear and develop colour. Then toss vigorously using a spatula or by wrist-flicking the wok. Stir-fry 2–3 minutes until 80% cooked. Push to the side.
step_6: Add vegetables in order of cook time: firm vegetables (carrot, broccoli) first, soft vegetables (bean sprouts, spinach) last. Stir-fry each 1–2 minutes, then combine everything. Add the sauce, toss vigorously for 30 seconds until everything is coated and the sauce has thickened slightly.
step_7: Serve immediately over steamed rice or noodles. Wok-fried dishes deteriorate quickly — the crispness and wok hei (breath of the wok) flavour are at their peak the moment it leaves the heat.

step_3: Remove the protein. Reduce heat to medium and sauté the mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery or regional equivalent) for 5–7 minutes, stirring, until softened and lightly coloured. Season lightly.

tips: Consume 2–3 hours before training. The 0g carbs provide slow-release fuel without GI distress.
ingredients_items: pork belly|coriander culantro|oca tuber|potato papa amarilla|white rice arroz|sesame seeds|lime|garlic|soy sauce|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Preheat the oven to 210 °C / 410 °F fan (or 230 °C / 450 °F conventional). Prepare the spice and herb paste: mix all dry spices, garlic, lemon zest, and enough oil to make a spreadable paste.
step_2: Score the protein 3–4 times on the thicker side — this allows the marinade to penetrate deeper and ensures even cooking. Rub the paste aggressively into all surfaces and into the scores. Marinate at room temperature for 15 minutes minimum.
step_3: Arrange vegetables in a single layer in a roasting dish. Drizzle with oil, season generously. Nestle the protein on top — elevated above the vegetables slightly so hot air circulates underneath.
step_4: Bake on the middle rack for 15 minutes at high heat to set the crust. Reduce to 180 °C / 350 °F and continue baking 10–20 minutes until the spice crust is fragrant and darkened, and the interior reaches the correct temperature.
step_5: If the crust browns too quickly, lay a piece of foil loosely over the top — do not seal it, just shield the surface. Remove foil for the final 5 minutes to re-crisp.
step_6: Squeeze lemon over the protein as it comes from the oven — the acid brightens all the spice flavours. Rest for 5 minutes.
step_7: Serve over the roasted vegetables with fresh herbs, yogurt or tahini sauce, and warm flatbread.

step_1: Prepare a herb crust: combine fresh herbs, garlic, zest, and a tablespoon of olive oil into a rough paste. Press firmly onto the top surface of the protein.
step_2: Preheat the grill to medium heat, 175–190 °C / 350–375 °F. Lower heat allows the herb crust to toast without burning and lets thicker cuts cook through.
step_3: Place the protein crust-side up on the grill (indirect if using gas) and cook with the lid closed for 8–12 minutes, depending on thickness — approximately 10 minutes per 2.5 cm / 1 inch.
step_4: Carefully flip and grill the crust side for 2–3 minutes over direct heat until golden and fragrant. Watch closely — herbs burn in seconds over high heat.
step_5: Verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest point away from bone. Target temperatures: 74 °C / 165 °F chicken; 70 °C / 158 °F pork; 63 °C / 145 °F fish.

step_7: Serve over the dressed vegetables or salad, with a wedge of citrus and a drizzle of best-quality finishing oil.

name: Anticucho Charcoal-Grilled Eggs with Coriander Culantro
description: A arequipa-style classic reimagined with eggs and aromatic huacatay — perfect for lunch.

step_1: Remove the protein from the refrigerator 20–30 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Cold protein dropped into a hot pan drops the pan temperature dramatically, resulting in steaming rather than searing.
step_2: Heat a heavy stainless-steel or cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat for 2–3 minutes until a water droplet dances and evaporates immediately. Add a thin film of neutral oil (grapeseed or sunflower) and heat until shimmering, just before smoking — approximately 200 °C / 400 °F.
step_3: Season the protein generously with flaky salt and fresh pepper on all sides immediately before it goes into the pan — not earlier, as salt draws moisture to the surface.
step_4: Lay the protein in the pan away from you to avoid oil splatter. Press gently with a spatula for 5 seconds to ensure full contact. Sear undisturbed for 3–4 minutes on medium-high heat until a deep golden-brown crust releases naturally from the pan.
step_5: Flip once. Add 2 tablespoons of butter, 2 garlic cloves, and a thyme sprig to the pan. Tilt the pan at a 30° angle and baste the protein continuously with the foaming butter for 90 seconds — this bastes, flavours, and accelerates cooking simultaneously.
step_6: Check doneness: fish flakes at 60–63 °C / 140–145 °F; chicken breast at 74 °C / 165 °F; duck breast at 57 °C / 135 °F (medium-rare). Use a thermometer — visual cues alone are unreliable.
step_7: Transfer to a wire rack set over a plate. Rest 3–5 minutes. Deglaze the pan with a splash of wine or stock, scraping up all fond (browned bits) to build an instant pan sauce. Pour over and serve.

step_1: Set up a two-zone grill: ignite one side to high heat (230–260 °C / 450–500 °F) and leave the other side unlit for indirect cooking. Let the grill heat for 10 minutes with the lid closed.
step_2: While the grill heats, pat the protein completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season generously with salt, pepper, and spices on all sides; press the seasoning in firmly.
step_3: Brush the grill grates with a high-smoke-point oil (grapeseed or refined avocado). Place the protein on the hot side. Do not move it for 2–3 minutes until grill marks release naturally — forcing it tears the crust.
step_4: Flip once and sear the second side for 2 minutes. Move to the indirect side, close the lid, and cook to the target internal temperature: 63 °C / 145 °F for fish; 74 °C / 165 °F for poultry; 57 °C / 135 °F for medium-rare beef or lamb.
step_5: While the protein finishes, grill the vegetables over direct medium heat (180 °C / 350 °F) for 3–5 minutes per side until lightly charred and just tender.
step_6: Rest the protein on a warm plate, tented loosely with foil, for 5 minutes (steaks) or 3 minutes (fish, chicken breast). Resting allows juices to redistribute — cutting too early loses up to 30 % of moisture.
step_7: Slice against the grain if applicable, arrange over the vegetables, and finish with the prepared sauce and fresh herbs immediately before serving.

step_1: Preheat your oven to 200 °C / 400 °F. Using an oven-safe skillet means you can sear on the stovetop and finish in the oven — the professional approach for thick cuts.

step_1: Heat the oven to 150 °C / 300 °F. In Italian slow-cooking, lower and slower is always better — the goal is collagen-to-gelatin conversion, which requires 2+ hours at 80–95 °C / 176–203 °F.

step_3: Raise heat to medium-high. Add the seasoned protein and sear 3–4 minutes per side. Remove. Add the tomatoes or wine, scrape the fond, and bring to a boil for 2 minutes.
step_4: Return the protein. The liquid should not cover the protein — add just enough to come halfway up. Tuck in fresh herbs and a Parmesan rind if available (it enriches the sauce with glutamates).
step_5: Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 2–3 hours. Every hour, turn the protein and baste with the surrounding juices. A properly braised Italian stew barely moves in the pot — it should tremble, not bubble.

step_2: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a wok or heavy pot over high heat. Add aromatics and stir-fry 30 seconds. Add Shaoxing wine or mirin, let it sizzle and reduce by half — about 30 seconds.
step_3: Add the braising liquid components: soy or tamari, sweet soy or palm sugar, star anise, cinnamon, ginger, and enough water or stock to half-submerge the protein. Bring to a strong boil.
step_4: Add the protein, reduce heat to medium-low, and braise partially covered for 1–2 hours, turning every 30 minutes. The liquid should simmer steadily — bubbling around the edges but not vigorously boiling, approximately 90–95 °C / 194–203 °F.
step_5: Remove the lid for the final 20 minutes and raise heat to medium. The sauce will reduce and coat the protein in a lacquered, glossy glaze — this finishing step is critical for the signature texture.
step_6: Check doneness: the protein should be pull-apart tender and the sauce should coat a spoon thickly. Remove aromatics (star anise, cinnamon) before serving.
step_7: Serve over steamed jasmine rice or hand-cut noodles. Spoon sauce generously over the top and finish with sliced spring onions and a drizzle of sesame oil.

step_1: The night before or at least 2 hours before cooking, marinate the protein in the prepared spice blend, citrus, and aromatics. Diana Kennedy insists this resting period is not optional — the acid in citrus begins to denature surface proteins, improving texture.
step_2: Sear the protein in batches in hot oil — lard in the traditional recipe, but a high-smoke-point oil works — over medium-high heat for 3–4 minutes per side until well browned. Do not crowd the pan. Browning is flavour.
step_3: Build the braising base: sauté onion, garlic, and peppers for 8 minutes over medium heat until soft. Add the dried or toasted chili paste and fry for 2 minutes, stirring, until darkened and fragrant.
step_4: Add the warm liquid (stock, beer, or a combination) and bring to a simmer, scraping the base of the pan. Return the protein, pushing it into the liquid. The liquid should reach two-thirds up the protein.

step_1: Set up a two-zone grill: ignite one side to high heat (230–260 °C / 450–500 °F) and leave the other side unlit for indirect cooking. Let the grill heat for 10 minutes with the lid closed.
step_2: While the grill heats, pat the protein completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season generously with salt, pepper, and spices on all sides; press the seasoning in firmly.
step_3: Brush the grill grates with a high-smoke-point oil (grapeseed or refined avocado). Place the protein on the hot side. Do not move it for 2–3 minutes until grill marks release naturally — forcing it tears the crust.
step_4: Flip once and sear the second side for 2 minutes. Move to the indirect side, close the lid, and cook to the target internal temperature: 63 °C / 145 °F for fish; 74 °C / 165 °F for poultry; 57 °C / 135 °F for medium-rare beef or lamb.
step_5: While the protein finishes, grill the vegetables over direct medium heat (180 °C / 350 °F) for 3–5 minutes per side until lightly charred and just tender.
step_6: Rest the protein on a warm plate, tented loosely with foil, for 5 minutes (steaks) or 3 minutes (fish, chicken breast). Resting allows juices to redistribute — cutting too early loses up to 30 % of moisture.
step_7: Slice against the grain if applicable, arrange over the vegetables, and finish with the prepared sauce and fresh herbs immediately before serving.

step_1: Fill the base of a wok or large pot with 4–5 cm of water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Steaming requires sustained, vigorous steam — not a quiet simmer.

step_3: Season the protein inside and out with salt, white pepper, and a drizzle of sesame oil. Place on the steaming vessel and add your sauce ingredients around the base.
step_4: Set the steamer basket over the boiling water, ensuring the base does not touch the water. Cover tightly with the lid — gaps allow steam to escape and reduce cooking temperatures.

step_3: Oil the grate and lay the protein down. Grill uncovered for 90 seconds, then rotate 45° to create a crosshatch; grill 90 seconds more. Flip and repeat on the second side.

step_1: Heat the oven to 150 °C / 300 °F. In Italian slow-cooking, lower and slower is always better — the goal is collagen-to-gelatin conversion, which requires 2+ hours at 80–95 °C / 176–203 °F.
step_2: In a heavy oven-safe casserole, heat olive oil over medium heat and sauté the soffritto (onion, celery, carrot) for 10 full minutes, stirring frequently, until golden and sweet — this is the foundation of Italian braising. Do not rush it.
step_3: Raise heat to medium-high. Add the seasoned protein and sear 3–4 minutes per side. Remove. Add the tomatoes or wine, scrape the fond, and bring to a boil for 2 minutes.
step_4: Return the protein. The liquid should not cover the protein — add just enough to come halfway up. Tuck in fresh herbs and a Parmesan rind if available (it enriches the sauce with glutamates).

tips: Pair with an additional portion of rice noodles mie to add 150–200 extra quality calories for a bulk phase.
ingredients_items: satay chicken skewers|bamboo shoots rebung|turmeric kunyit fresh|young coconut kelapa muda|lontong compressed rice|peanut sauce bumbu kacang|daun salam bay|candlenut|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Fill the base of a wok or large pot with 4–5 cm of water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Steaming requires sustained, vigorous steam — not a quiet simmer.
step_2: Prepare the steaming vessel: line a bamboo steamer basket or heatproof plate with spring onion batons and ginger slices. These aromatics perfume the steam and prevent sticking.
step_3: Season the protein inside and out with salt, white pepper, and a drizzle of sesame oil. Place on the steaming vessel and add your sauce ingredients around the base.
step_4: Set the steamer basket over the boiling water, ensuring the base does not touch the water. Cover tightly with the lid — gaps allow steam to escape and reduce cooking temperatures.
step_5: Steam over high heat for 8–12 minutes depending on thickness (6 minutes for a 2 cm fish fillet; 12 minutes for a 4 cm thick cut). A properly steamed protein cooks at 100 °C / 212 °F — faster and more gentle than oven heat.
step_6: Test doneness: the flesh should flake at the thickest point when pressed with a chopstick; the internal temperature should read 63 °C / 145 °F for fish. Do not overcook — oversteamed fish turns cottony within 60 seconds of its target temperature.
step_7: Slide the steamed protein and all its juices onto a warmed plate. Heat 3 tablespoons of neutral oil in a small pan over high heat until smoking — 230 °C / 450 °F. Scatter fresh ginger and spring onion over the fish and pour the smoking oil over: it will sizzle and spit, flash-cooking the aromatics. Finish with soy sauce and serve.

name: Bumbu Rempah-Spiced Eggs Telur Balado with Bamboo Shoots Rebung
description: A javanese classic reimagined with eggs telur balado and aromatic daun salam bay — perfect for lunch.
tips: Pair with an additional portion of cassava singkong to add 150–200 extra quality calories for a bulk phase.
ingredients_items: eggs telur balado|bamboo shoots rebung|chili rawit bird eye|turmeric kunyit fresh|cassava singkong|fried tofu pressed|daun salam bay|kecap manis sweet soy|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Prepare all ingredients before any heat is applied — stir-frying happens in under 5 minutes and there is no time to stop and cut once you begin. Slice protein thinly (5 mm / ¼ inch), cut vegetables to uniform size.
step_2: Season the protein: toss with 1 teaspoon cornstarch, a pinch of salt, and a dash of soy sauce. The cornstarch creates a light coating that protects moisture and helps the sauce cling.
step_3: Heat a seasoned wok over the highest possible flame — a properly heated wok surface reaches 300–370 °C / 570–700 °F. Add 2 tablespoons of oil in a clockwise swirl around the sides. When thin wisps of smoke rise from the oil, the wok is ready.
step_4: Add the aromatics (garlic, ginger, dried chili). Stir constantly for 15–20 seconds — aromatics burn in 30 seconds at this temperature. Their fragrance signals they are ready.
step_5: Add the protein in a single layer. Do not stir for 60 seconds — let it sear and develop colour. Then toss vigorously using a spatula or by wrist-flicking the wok. Stir-fry 2–3 minutes until 80% cooked. Push to the side.
step_6: Add vegetables in order of cook time: firm vegetables (carrot, broccoli) first, soft vegetables (bean sprouts, spinach) last. Stir-fry each 1–2 minutes, then combine everything. Add the sauce, toss vigorously for 30 seconds until everything is coated and the sauce has thickened slightly.
step_7: Serve immediately over steamed rice or noodles. Wok-fried dishes deteriorate quickly — the crispness and wok hei (breath of the wok) flavour are at their peak the moment it leaves the heat.

description: A hard indonesian main featuring beef dendeng cooked slow cooked with kecap manis sweet soy, terasi shrimp paste and fresh shrimp paste terasi.

step_1: The night before or at least 2 hours before cooking, marinate the protein in the prepared spice blend, citrus, and aromatics. Diana Kennedy insists this resting period is not optional — the acid in citrus begins to denature surface proteins, improving texture.
step_2: Sear the protein in batches in hot oil — lard in the traditional recipe, but a high-smoke-point oil works — over medium-high heat for 3–4 minutes per side until well browned. Do not crowd the pan. Browning is flavour.
step_3: Build the braising base: sauté onion, garlic, and peppers for 8 minutes over medium heat until soft. Add the dried or toasted chili paste and fry for 2 minutes, stirring, until darkened and fragrant.
step_4: Add the warm liquid (stock, beer, or a combination) and bring to a simmer, scraping the base of the pan. Return the protein, pushing it into the liquid. The liquid should reach two-thirds up the protein.
step_5: Cook covered at the lowest possible heat — the surface should show just an occasional lazy bubble, 85–90 °C / 185–195 °F. This is below a simmer and prevents the muscle fibres from seizing and becoming tough.
step_6: Cook for 2–4 hours, turning every 60 minutes, until the protein falls apart at the touch of a fork. Remove the protein and shred with two forks. Reduce the sauce over medium heat for 10 minutes until thick enough to coat a spoon.

step_2: In a heavy oven-safe casserole, heat olive oil over medium heat and sauté the soffritto (onion, celery, carrot) for 10 full minutes, stirring frequently, until golden and sweet — this is the foundation of Italian braising. Do not rush it.
step_3: Raise heat to medium-high. Add the seasoned protein and sear 3–4 minutes per side. Remove. Add the tomatoes or wine, scrape the fond, and bring to a boil for 2 minutes.
step_4: Return the protein. The liquid should not cover the protein — add just enough to come halfway up. Tuck in fresh herbs and a Parmesan rind if available (it enriches the sauce with glutamates).
step_5: Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 2–3 hours. Every hour, turn the protein and baste with the surrounding juices. A properly braised Italian stew barely moves in the pot — it should tremble, not bubble.

step_1: Preheat the oven to 120 °C / 250 °F. Low-temperature roasting cooks the protein edge to edge at a uniform temperature — a technique popularised by Heston Blumenthal and J. Kenji López-Alt.

step_5: Sear the protein in the scorching-hot pan for 60–90 seconds per side, or under the broiler 5 cm from the element for 2–3 minutes per side, until the crust is deep brown.
step_6: Rest for only 5 minutes — since the interior was cooked slowly, less resting is needed. The juices are already set.

tips: Add an extra 64g of pork intestines for isaw to boost protein to ~35g per serving on heavy training days.
ingredients_items: pork intestines for isaw|garlic bawang|sitaw long beans|green mango manggang hilaw|banana blossom puso ng saging|ensaymada sweet bread|coconut vinegar suka|fish sauce patis|calamansi lime|garlic bawang|sea salt|black pepper
step_1: Preheat the oven to 160 °C / 325 °F — low enough to dissolve collagen into gelatin over time without toughening the muscle fibres. Pat the protein completely dry; wet protein will steam, not brown.
step_2: Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat, 200 °C / 400 °F on the surface. Brown the protein in batches for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply mahogany. This Maillard reaction creates the complex flavour base for the entire braise.
step_3: Remove the protein. Reduce heat to medium and sauté the mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery or regional equivalent) for 5–7 minutes, stirring, until softened and lightly coloured. Season lightly.
step_4: Add tomato paste or spice paste and stir for 1–2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick — cooking out the raw taste. Deglaze with wine, stock, or water and scrape all the fond from the bottom.
step_5: Nestle the protein into the braising liquid. The liquid should reach halfway up the protein, never submerge it — you are braising, not boiling. Bring to a gentle simmer on the stovetop.
step_6: Cover with a tight lid and transfer to the oven. Braise for 1.5–3 hours depending on the cut — it is done when a fork slides in and twists with zero resistance, not just when it's tender. Turn the protein every 45 minutes for even cooking.
step_7: Remove the protein. Strain the braising liquid, skim the fat, and reduce over medium-high heat for 5–8 minutes until glossy and sauce-like. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve the protein with sauce spooned over and fresh herbs.

step_1: The night before or at least 2 hours before cooking, marinate the protein in the prepared spice blend, citrus, and aromatics. Diana Kennedy insists this resting period is not optional — the acid in citrus begins to denature surface proteins, improving texture.

step_4: Add the warm liquid (stock, beer, or a combination) and bring to a simmer, scraping the base of the pan. Return the protein, pushing it into the liquid. The liquid should reach two-thirds up the protein.

step_1: Fill the base of a wok or large pot with 4–5 cm of water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Steaming requires sustained, vigorous steam — not a quiet simmer.
step_2: Prepare the steaming vessel: line a bamboo steamer basket or heatproof plate with spring onion batons and ginger slices. These aromatics perfume the steam and prevent sticking.
step_3: Season the protein inside and out with salt, white pepper, and a drizzle of sesame oil. Place on the steaming vessel and add your sauce ingredients around the base.
step_4: Set the steamer basket over the boiling water, ensuring the base does not touch the water. Cover tightly with the lid — gaps allow steam to escape and reduce cooking temperatures.
step_5: Steam over high heat for 8–12 minutes depending on thickness (6 minutes for a 2 cm fish fillet; 12 minutes for a 4 cm thick cut). A properly steamed protein cooks at 100 °C / 212 °F — faster and more gentle than oven heat.
step_6: Test doneness: the flesh should flake at the thickest point when pressed with a chopstick; the internal temperature should read 63 °C / 145 °F for fish. Do not overcook — oversteamed fish turns cottony within 60 seconds of its target temperature.
step_7: Slide the steamed protein and all its juices onto a warmed plate. Heat 3 tablespoons of neutral oil in a small pan over high heat until smoking — 230 °C / 450 °F. Scatter fresh ginger and spring onion over the fish and pour the smoking oil over: it will sizzle and spit, flash-cooking the aromatics. Finish with soy sauce and serve.

step_1: Slice the protein thinly against the grain (5 mm / ¼ inch) for maximum surface area and faster, more even cooking — a technique seen throughout Nobu Matsuhisa's and David Chang's kitchens.
step_2: Marinate slices for 15 minutes at room temperature in the prepared sauce. Remove and pat semi-dry — excess marinade burns in the hot pan before the protein cooks.
step_3: Heat a carbon-steel or cast-iron skillet over the highest possible heat for 3 minutes. The pan should be hot enough to char a sprinkle of flour instantly. Add oil and heat until smoking.

step_5: Reduce heat to medium. Add aromatics (garlic, ginger, chili) to the same pan and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the sauce and bring to a vigorous boil for 1 minute to reduce and concentrate.
step_6: Return the protein and any resting juices to the pan. Toss over medium-high heat for 30 seconds until the sauce coats every piece and begins to caramelise at the edges.
step_7: Serve immediately over prepared grains or noodles. Garnish with fresh herbs, sesame seeds, or pickled vegetables.

step_1: Prepare the aromatics: bruise lemongrass stalks with the back of a knife to release the oils. Tear kaffir lime leaves. These will infuse the steam with their volatile aromatics.

step_1: The night before or at least 2 hours before cooking, marinate the protein in the prepared spice blend, citrus, and aromatics. Diana Kennedy insists this resting period is not optional — the acid in citrus begins to denature surface proteins, improving texture.
step_2: Sear the protein in batches in hot oil — lard in the traditional recipe, but a high-smoke-point oil works — over medium-high heat for 3–4 minutes per side until well browned. Do not crowd the pan. Browning is flavour.
step_3: Build the braising base: sauté onion, garlic, and peppers for 8 minutes over medium heat until soft. Add the dried or toasted chili paste and fry for 2 minutes, stirring, until darkened and fragrant.
step_4: Add the warm liquid (stock, beer, or a combination) and bring to a simmer, scraping the base of the pan. Return the protein, pushing it into the liquid. The liquid should reach two-thirds up the protein.
step_5: Cook covered at the lowest possible heat — the surface should show just an occasional lazy bubble, 85–90 °C / 185–195 °F. This is below a simmer and prevents the muscle fibres from seizing and becoming tough.
step_6: Cook for 2–4 hours, turning every 60 minutes, until the protein falls apart at the touch of a fork. Remove the protein and shred with two forks. Reduce the sauce over medium heat for 10 minutes until thick enough to coat a spoon.
step_7: Combine the shredded protein with half the sauce. Serve in warm tortillas or over rice with the remaining sauce, pickled onions, fresh coriander, and lime.

step_1: Toast whole spices (cumin seeds, coriander seeds, cardamom) in a dry pan over medium heat for 60–90 seconds until fragrant and beginning to pop. Grind in a mortar — freshly ground spice has 3× the aromatic impact of pre-ground.

step_4: Add the ground spices and tomato or tamarind base. Stir constantly for 2 minutes over medium heat, frying the paste until it darkens and pulls away from the sides of the pot.
step_5: Return the protein. Add enough warm liquid (stock, coconut milk, or tomato) to reach halfway up the sides. Bring to a bubbling simmer, then reduce heat to the lowest possible setting — the surface should barely tremor.
